A dependent expressing possession or another relation, often English “of.”

“In the beginning”: a supplied temporal use of on, with dative anginne.
“Created,” third-person singular preterite. In the opening, the subject God follows the verb; word order alone does not identify the object.
“Heaven”: accusative singular of weak feminine heofone, a variant of the masculine heofon learned above. It is not masculine heofon's plural.
Connective “now/for its part”; “empty and void.” The two adjectives are predicate feminine nominative singular with eorðe.
Ofer means “over” and here requires a dative head. Apply the nested-genitive construction of §9 to identify the head and its dependent.

“Was borne/carried over the waters,” contextually “moved over the waters.” Wæs gefęred is a passive phrase; gefęred is a past participle. Here ofer has accusative plural wæteru, unlike the preceding dative construction.
“Then said”: cwæð is third-person singular preterite; this ðā is the adverb “then,” not the article.
“Let light come to be.” Geweorðe is a finite third-person singular present subjunctive (also called optative), expressing a wish or command.
“Light was made/came into being.” Wearð is a third-person singular preterite used here with past participle geworht in a passive phrase.
geseah ðā ðæt hit gōd wæs

“Then saw that it was good.” Geseah is third-person singular preterite; ðā is “then”; ðæt is the conjunction “that.” Gōd is a neuter nominative singular predicate adjective. The copula stands at the end of the embedded clause. Use the context and §8 for the reference of hit.
Gedǣlde is “separated,” third-person singular preterite. Identify the reference of the subject pronoun from the preceding clause. The object and fram phrase use §9.
hēt ðæt lēoht Dæg, and ðā ðīestru Niht

“[He] called the light Day, and the darkness Night.” Hēt is third-person singular preterite, with God/he understood as subject. Ðæt lēoht and ðā ðīestru are accusative objects; Dæg and Niht are accusative names applied to them. Here ðæt and ðā are articles.
Ðā wæs geworden ǣfen and morgen ān dæg.

“Then there came to be evening and morning: one day.” Wæs geworden expresses a resulting state or completed coming-to-be, “had come to be”; geworden is a past participle. Ān dæg is “one day,” not the ordinal “first day.” Treat this closing formula as a whole.
